Multifactor Analysis MFA

Antonio Miñarro (aminarro@ub.edu)

30 setembre, 2025

1 Introduction to Multifactor Analysis (MFA)

1.1 What is MFA?

Multifactor Analysis (MFA) is a multivariate analysis technique that allows analyzing data sets where variables are organized into groups. This technique is useful for identifying common structures between groups and the specificities of each group.

It is especially useful when groups of variables have different units of measurement or importance.

This method is an extension of PCA (Principal Component Analysis), but considers information structured into blocks of variables.

mfa1

1.2 Why use MFA?

  • Integration of multiple data sources: Allows combining data from different sources or blocks of variables.
  • Group comparison: Facilitates the comparison of results from several principal component analyses (PCA) or multiple correspondence analyses (MCA) in a single frame of reference.
  • Identification of common structures: Helps identify common structures and specificities between groups of variables.

1.3 Objectives

  • Study the similarity between individuals with respect to the entire set of variables AND the relationships between variables.

1.3.1 Take into account group structure

  • Study the general similarities and differences between groups (and the specific characteristics of each group).
  • Study the similarities and differences between groups from an individual point of view.
  • Compare the characteristics of individuals based on separate analyses.

⇒ Balance the influence of all groups in the analysis.

1.4 How an MFA works

MFA starts from the same principle as PCA, but incorporates groups of variables \(G_1, G_2, \dots, G_J\), each with \(p_j\) variables and a total of I individuals in the sample.

  • In a PCA, normalization balances the influence of each variable

  • In an MFA, we balance in terms of groups

A MFA is a PCA weighted by the variability of the groups

1.4.1 Weighting of each group

Each group of variables is normalized so that its total inertia is 1. Inertia is defined as the sum of the eigenvariances:

The total inertia of the cloud of individuals (identical to that of the cloud of variables) can be expressed, highlighting the role of each group of variables (we assume that the data are centered) as \[\text{Total inertia} = \sum_i d^2(O, i) = \sum_i \sum_k z_{ik}^2 = \sum_j \sum_{k \in K_j} \sum_i z_{ik}^2 = \sum_j \sum_{k \in K_j} Var[k]\]

\[ \text{Total intertia} = \sum_{i=1}^{p_J} \lambda_i \]

To ensure that each group has the same contribution, we divide its data by the first eigenvalue of its individual PCA:

  • We calculate the first eigenvalue \(\lambda_1^j\) of the group \(j\) of variables \((j=1,...,J)\)

  • We perform a global PCA on the transformed data

\[\left( \frac{Z_1}{\sqrt{\lambda_1^1}};\frac{Z_2}{\sqrt{\lambda_1^2}};...;\frac{Z_J}{\sqrt{\lambda_1^J}} \right)\] The \(Z_j\) would be the normalized data of a group of variables.

\[ Z_j^* = \frac{Z_j}{\sqrt{\lambda_1^j}} \]

where \(\lambda_1^j\) is the first eigenvalue of the PCA of the group \(j\).

1.4.2 Global PCA

Once the groups have been rescaled, the information is concatenated into a new normalized matrix:

\[ Z^* = [Z_1^* | Z_2^* | \dots | Z_J^*] \]

and a global PCA is performed on \(Z^*\), obtaining balanced principal components between groups.

  • The weights are the same for all variables in the same group: the group structure is preserved.

  • For each group, the variance of the first dimension (first eigenvalue) is equal to 1.

1.5 Key differences between PCA and MFA

Method Input matrix Initial weighting Component calculation
PCA Data matrix \(X\) All variables equal \(S v = \lambda v\)
MFA Concatenated matrix \(Z^*\) Each group weighted by \(\lambda_1^j\) Global PCA over \(Z^*\)

In an MFA we have data structured into groups and we want to make sure that no group dominates the analysis.

2 The FactoMineR package

The FactoMineR package in R is a powerful tool for performing MFA. It provides functions for exploratory analysis of multivariate data and data mining.

2.1 Example dataset

We will work with some metabolic syndrome data obtained from Kaggle https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/antimoni/metabolic-syndrome

This dataset contains information about people with metabolic syndrome, a complex medical condition associated with a cluster of risk factors for cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. The data include demographic, clinical, and laboratory measures, as well as the presence or absence of metabolic syndrome.

To facilitate interpretation, we randomly select 50 individuals from the original set.

set.seed(1234)
dades<-read.csv("Metabolic Syndrome.csv")
dades$Marital[dades$Marital==""]<-NA
dades<-dades[complete.cases(dades),]
dades<-dades[sample(1:nrow(dades),50),]
dades$MetabolicSyndrome<-as.factor(dades$MetabolicSyndrome)
for (i in c(3,4,6)) dades[,i]<-as.factor(dades[,i])
DT::datatable(dades)

2.1.1 Running the Analysis

The basic function call is

MFA (base, group, type = rep("s",length(group)), ind.sup = NULL, 
    name.group = NULL, num.group.sup = NULL, graph = TRUE)

  • base : a data frame with n rows (individuals) and p columns (variables)

  • group: a vector with the number of variables in each group.

  • type: the type of variables in each group. By default, all variables are quantitative and scaled to unit variance. Allowed values include:

    • “c” or “s” for quantitative variables. If “s”, the variables are scaled to unit variance.
    • “n” for categorical variables.
    • “f” for frequencies (from a contingency tables).

  • ind.sup: a vector indicating the indexes of the supplementary individuals.

  • name.group: a vector containing the name of the groups (by default, NULL and the group are named group.1, group.2 and so on).

*num.group.sup: the indexes of the illustrative groups (by default, NULL and no group are illustrative).

*graph : a logical value. If TRUE a graph is displayed.

library(FactoMineR)
library(factoextra)

dades2mfa<-dades[,c(2,5,7,8,10:15)]
group<-c(2,2,5,1)
type<-c('s','s','s','n')
name.group<-c('Socio','clini','fisio','synd')
dades.mfa<-MFA(dades2mfa,group=group,type=type,name.group = name.group,graph = FALSE,num.group.sup = 4)

2.1.3 Groups of variables

The functions get_mfa or get_mfa_var allow you to extract information from individuals, qualitative or quantitative variables, groups or partial axes of the analysis.

get_mfa(
  res.mfa,
  element = c("ind", "quanti.var", "quali.var", "group", "partial.axes")
)

get_mfa_var(res.mfa, element = c("quanti.var", "quali.var", "group"))
group <- get_mfa_var(dades.mfa, "group")
group
## Multiple Factor Analysis results for variable groups 
##  ===================================================
##   Name           Description                                          
## 1 "$coord"       "Coordinates"                                        
## 2 "$cos2"        "Cos2, quality of representation"                    
## 3 "$contrib"     "Contributions"                                      
## 4 "$correlation" "Correlation between groups and principal dimensions"
# Coordinates of groups
head(group$coord)

# Cos2: quality of representation on the factore map
head(group$cos2)

fviz_mfa_var(dades.mfa, "group")

  • red color = active groups of variables

  • green color = supplementary groups of variables

If two groups of variables have approximately the same coordinates in a dimension, it means that their contribution is similar in that dimension.

We can extract the specific contribution of each group of variables with the function

# Contribution to the first dimension
fviz_contrib(dades.mfa, "group", axes = 1)

# Contribution to the second dimension
fviz_contrib(dades.mfa, "group", axes = 2)

Correlation between quantitative variables and dimensions. The R code below plots quantitative variables colored by groups. The argument palette is used to change group colors. Supplementary quantitative variables are in dashed arrow and violet color. We use repel = TRUE, to avoid text overlapping.

fviz_mfa_var(dades.mfa, "quanti.var", palette = "jco", 
             col.var.sup = "violet", repel = TRUE)

To make the plot more readable, we can use geom = c(“point”, “text”) instead of geom = c(“arrow”, “text”). We’ll change also the legend position from “right” to “bottom”, using the argument legend = “bottom”:

fviz_mfa_var(dades.mfa, "quanti.var", palette = "jco", 
             col.var.sup = "violet", repel = TRUE,
             geom = c("point", "text"), legend = "bottom")

Briefly, the graph of variables (correlation circle) shows the relationship between variables, the quality of the representation of variables, as well as, the correlation between variables and the dimensions:

  • Positive correlated variables are grouped together, whereas negative ones are positioned on opposite sides of the plot origin (opposed quadrants).

  • The distance between variable points and the origin measures the quality of the variable on the factor map. Variable points that are away from the origin are well represented on the factor map.

  • For a given dimension, the most correlated variables to the dimension are close to the dimension.

The contribution of quantitative variables (in %) to the definition of the dimensions can be visualized using the function fviz_contrib() [factoextra package]. Variables are colored by groups. The R code below shows the top 10 variable categories contributing to the dimensions:

# Contributions to dimension 1
fviz_contrib(dades.mfa, choice = "quanti.var", axes = 1, top = 10,
             palette = "jco")

# Contributions to dimension 2
fviz_contrib(dades.mfa, choice = "quanti.var", axes = 2, top = 10,
             palette = "jco")

The red dashed line on the graph above indicates the expected average value, If the contributions were uniform.

The most contributing quantitative variables can be highlighted on the scatter plot using the argument col.var = “contrib”. This produces a gradient colors, which can be customized using the argument gradient.cols.

fviz_mfa_var(dades.mfa, "quanti.var", col.var = "contrib", 
             gradient.cols = c("#00AFBB", "#E7B800", "#FC4E07"), 
             col.var.sup = "violet", repel = TRUE,
             geom = c("point", "text"))

Similarly, we can highlight quantitative variables using their cos2 values that represent the quality of representation in the factor map.

The quality of this representation is measured by the squared value of the cosine (\(cos^2\)) of the angle of the triangle formed by the origin point, the observation and the projection onto the component. For a given variable, the sum of the \(cos^2\) over all dimensions will be equal to 1, and if in addition the variable is perfectly representable by only the first two dimensions, the sum of cos2 over these two will be equal to 1. Variables positioned near the origin may be an indication that more than two dimensions would be needed for their representation.

# Color by cos2 values: quality on the factor map
fviz_mfa_var(dades.mfa, col.var = "cos2",
             gradient.cols = c("#00AFBB", "#E7B800", "#FC4E07"), 
             col.var.sup = "violet", repel = TRUE)

To create a bar plot of variables cos2, type this:

fviz_cos2(dades.mfa, choice = "quanti.var", axes = 1)

2.1.5 Plotting individuals

To obtain the information of individuals

ind <- get_mfa_ind(dades.mfa)
ind
## Multiple Factor Analysis results for individuals 
##  ===================================================
##   Name                      Description                      
## 1 "$coord"                  "Coordinates"                    
## 2 "$cos2"                   "Cos2, quality of representation"
## 3 "$contrib"                "Contributions"                  
## 4 "$coord.partiel"          "Partial coordinates"            
## 5 "$within.inertia"         "Within inertia"                 
## 6 "$within.partial.inertia" "Within partial inertia"

For instance

head(ind$coord)
##           Dim.1      Dim.2       Dim.3      Dim.4      Dim.5
## 1564 -0.4789299  0.5843612 -1.23962748 -0.1957296 -0.1921185
## 2230 -1.1264470 -0.4633751 -0.99260849 -0.8455583  0.1516074
## 1235  0.3304260  1.9214711 -0.08787666  0.8880198  0.5279605
## 2314 -1.0997807  0.6138582 -1.43716994  0.5393967  0.3267869
## 1361  1.3936084 -1.0868654 -0.28575537 -0.8662260 -0.7132505
## 1218 -1.3101630 -0.7871862 -0.39798989 -0.9998127 -0.1172876

To plot individuals, use the function fviz_mfa_ind() [in factoextra]. By default, individuals are colored in blue. However, like variables, it’s also possible to color individuals by their cos2 values:

fviz_mfa_ind(dades.mfa, col.ind = "cos2", 
             gradient.cols = c("#00AFBB", "#E7B800", "#FC4E07"),
             repel = TRUE)

Note that, it’s possible to color the individuals using any of the qualitative variables in the initial data table. To do this, the argument habillage is used in the fviz_mfa_ind() function. For example, if you want to color the wines according to the supplementary qualitative variable “MetabolicSyndrome”, type this:

fviz_mfa_ind(dades.mfa, 
             habillage = "MetabolicSyndrome", # color by groups 
             palette = c("#00AFBB", "#E7B800", "#FC4E07"),
             addEllipses = TRUE, ellipse.type = "confidence", 
             repel = TRUE # Avoid text overlapping
             )

Other kinds of ellipses:

  • “convex”: plot convex hull of a set o points.

  • “confidence”: plot confidence ellipses arround group mean points as coord.ellipse()[in FactoMineR].

  • “t”: assumes a multivariate t-distribution.

  • “norm”: assumes a multivariate normal distribution. (És l’opció per defecte)

  • “euclid”: draws a circle with the radius equal to level, representing the euclidean distance from the center. This ellipse probably won’t appear circular unless coord_fixed() is applied.

If we have more than one categorical variable we can do the simultaneous representation

fviz_ellipses(dades.mfa, c("MetabolicSyndrome","MetabolicSyndrome"), repel = TRUE,ellipse.type = "convex")

2.1.6 Partial Individuals Plot

The results for individuals obtained from the analysis performed with a single group are called partial individuals. In other words, an individual considered from the point of view of a single group is called a partial individual.

In the fviz_mfa_ind() plot, by default, for a given individual, the point corresponds to the average or the center of gravity of the individual’s partial points. That is, the individual seen by all groups of variables.

For a given individual, there are as many partial points as there are groups of variables.

The partial individuals plot represents each individual seen by each group and its center of gravity.

To represent the partial points of all individuals we use

fviz_mfa_ind(dades.mfa, partial = "all")

But if we want only some individuals

fviz_mfa_ind(dades.mfa, partial = c("1293", "681"),alpha.ind=0.2)

o

fviz_mfa_ind(dades.mfa, partial = c("1293", "681"),select.ind = list(names=c("1293", "681")))

We can also achieve the representation with the plot.MFA function which allows us to further customize the output and specify for example whether the groups represent time instants (chrono=TRUE) with which we can visualize the temporal evolution of each individual.

plot(dades.mfa,partial=c("1293", "681"),chrono=T,select=c("1293", "681"))

2.1.7 Partial axes graph

The partial axes graph shows the relationship between the main axes of the MFA and those obtained from the analysis of each group using a PCA (for groups of continuous variables) or an MCA (for qualitative variables).

fviz_mfa_axes(dades.mfa)

2.2 Additional interpretation of the axes

We can calculate the correlations of each variable with the axes and perform hypothesis testing

dimdesc(dades.mfa)
## $Dim.1
## 
## Link between the variable and the continuous variables (R-square)
## =================================================================================
##               correlation      p.value
## Triglycerides   0.6868974 3.626793e-08
## WaistCirc       0.6521762 2.881440e-07

3 Separate results for each group (PCA or MCA)

All results are accessible for each group separately just as if we had done a PCA or MCA on each group of variables.

For example if we focus on the group of physiological variables

4 Analysis with groups of qualitative variables

The methodology is the same but replaces PCA with Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA)

We can see an example of MCA in the following document MCA.html

dades2mfa.2<-dades[,c(3,4,6,2,5,7,8,10:15)]
group<-c(3,2,2,5,1)
type<-c('n','s','s','s','n')
name.group<-c('carac','Socio','clini','fisio','synd')
dades.mfa.2<-MFA(dades2mfa.2,group=group,type=type,name.group = name.group,graph = F,num.group.sup = 5)

4.1 Summary of results
